sections.title: SDLC — Software Development Life Cycle
sections.blurb: How an idea becomes running software: the phases every team walks through, and the two ways of walking through them.

concepts.name: The 7 phases
concepts.tagline: Requirement → Analysis → Design → Development → Testing → Deployment → Maintenance
concepts.analogy: Building software is like building a house: agree what the family needs, draw the plans, build it, inspect it, hand over the keys, then keep fixing the leaks.
explanation: SDLC is simply an agreed order of work. Each phase produces something the next phase consumes: requirements produce a document, design produces diagrams, development produces code, testing produces a verdict.
The value is not the ceremony — it is that mistakes get cheaper the earlier you catch them. A misunderstood requirement costs minutes to fix on paper and weeks to fix in production.
Maintenance is not the end of the road. Real products loop back to requirements with what they learned from live users, which is exactly what Agile formalises.
useWhen: You want a shared vocabulary for where a project currently stands
You need sign-off gates for regulated or fixed-price work
You are planning cost and timeline before writing code

steps.caption: Talk to the people who will use the product and write down what they need.
Check the idea is possible in the time, money and skills available.
Draw the system: modules, database tables, APIs, screens.
Engineers implement the design, review each other's code and merge it.
Unit, integration and user-acceptance tests prove the build behaves.
Release to production — usually automated through a CI/CD pipeline.
Monitor, patch and enhance. What you learn here becomes the next round of requirements.
steps.output: a living product, not a finished project

concepts.springNote: In a Spring Boot project the later phases are mostly automation: profiles for each environment, actuator for monitoring in maintenance.

concepts.name: Waterfall vs Agile
concepts.tagline: One big delivery, or many small ones
concepts.analogy: Waterfall is ordering a full wedding cake months ahead. Agile is baking one tier at a time and tasting after each.
explanation: Waterfall runs the phases once, top to bottom. It is predictable and easy to contract, but the customer only sees working software at the very end — so a wrong assumption survives the whole project.
Agile runs the same phases in short iterations (sprints of 1-4 weeks). Every sprint ends with something demoable, so feedback arrives while it is still cheap to act on.
Neither is universally right. Fixed scope and regulatory sign-off favour waterfall; unclear or evolving scope favours agile.
useWhen: Waterfall: requirements are frozen, e.g. compliance or hardware-bound work
Agile: the product is discovering its market and priorities shift
Hybrid: fixed architecture up front, iterative feature delivery after
concepts.differsFrom: Agile is not 'no planning' and waterfall is not 'no feedback'. The real difference is batch size: waterfall validates once at the end, agile validates every sprint.

steps.caption: Waterfall would do all planning here, once. Agile plans only the next two weeks.
Build one thin, usable slice — login, not the whole account system.
Demo it to real users at the end of the sprint.
Feedback reorders the backlog: some ideas are dropped before being built.
Ship the increment and start the loop again — value arrives every sprint.

concepts.springNote: Agile delivery leans on feature flags so half-finished work can ship safely behind a switch.

sections.title: SOLID principles
sections.blurb: Five habits that keep object-oriented code easy to change. Each one is a rule about where change is allowed to hurt.

concepts.name: S — Single Responsibility
concepts.tagline: A class should have one reason to change
concepts.analogy: A restaurant does not ask the chef to also drive deliveries and do the accounts — each person owns one job, so changing the menu never breaks the books.
explanation: 'Responsibility' means a reason to change, not a method count. If the accounting team and the marketing team can both force you to edit the same class, that class has two responsibilities.
Splitting them means a change to invoice formatting cannot accidentally break email sending, and each part can be tested on its own.
useWhen: A class name contains 'And' or 'Manager' and keeps growing
Unrelated teams keep editing the same file
Unit tests need a lot of unrelated mocks to run
concepts.differsFrom: SRP splits a class by reason-to-change; Interface Segregation splits an interface by who calls it. SRP is about the implementation, ISP about the contract.

steps.caption: One class does the maths, the formatting and the emailing.
Tax law changes — you edit the class. Risk: you could break the emails.
Extract the calculation into its own class.
Extract formatting and sending too.
Now a tax change touches only the calculator; email code stays untouched.
steps.output: one reason to change per class

concepts.springNote: Spring makes SRP cheap: each responsibility is a bean, wired in through the constructor.

concepts.name: O — Open/Closed
concepts.tagline: Open for extension, closed for modification
concepts.analogy: A power socket lets you plug in any new appliance without rewiring the wall. New behaviour arrives as a plug, not as a renovation.
explanation: Adding a feature should mean adding a class, not editing a switch statement that already works in production. Every edit to tested code is a chance to break it.
The trick is to depend on an abstraction (an interface) and let each new case be a new implementation the framework discovers.
useWhen: A long if/else or switch grows every time the business adds a case
Payment methods, discount rules, export formats, notification channels
You must extend behaviour without redeploying core logic
concepts.differsFrom: Strategy is the pattern most often used to achieve OCP; OCP is the goal, Strategy is one way to reach it.

steps.caption: Old code branches on a string: adding UPI means editing tested code.
Introduce an interface that describes 'a way to pay'.
The existing card flow becomes one implementation.
UPI arrives as a brand-new class. Nothing existing is edited.
The caller still talks to the interface, so it never changed at all.
steps.output: extend by adding, not by editing

concepts.springNote: Injecting a List of an interface is Spring's built-in Open/Closed mechanism — a new @Component joins the list automatically.

concepts.name: L — Liskov Substitution
concepts.tagline: A subclass must be usable anywhere its parent is
concepts.analogy: If a shop advertises 'any bird', it should not hand you a penguin when you asked for something to deliver a letter. A substitute must keep the promises of the original.
explanation: Inheritance is a promise: 'wherever you use the parent, you can use me'. Breaking that promise means callers must start checking types, which defeats polymorphism.

The classic smells are a subclass that throws UnsupportedOperationException, strengthens preconditions, or silently changes behaviour — like a Square that breaks a Rectangle's independent width and height.
useWhen: Deciding between inheritance and composition
A subclass overrides a method to do nothing or to throw
Callers use instanceof to work around a specific subclass
concepts.differsFrom: LSP is about behaviour, not compilation. Code can compile perfectly and still violate LSP the moment a caller's assumption breaks at runtime.

steps.caption: Client sets width 5, height 4 and expects area 20.
Given a Square, setting height also changes width — area becomes 16.
The client did nothing wrong, yet its assumption broke: LSP is violated.
Fix by modelling both as immutable Shapes with an area() method instead.
Now every implementation keeps the contract and substitution is safe.

concepts.name: I — Interface Segregation
concepts.tagline: No client should depend on methods it never calls
concepts.analogy: A restaurant gives vegetarians a veg menu, not one giant book where half the pages are irrelevant and confusing.
explanation: A fat interface forces every implementer to provide methods it does not need, usually by throwing or returning null — which then breaks Liskov too.
Small, role-based interfaces let a class implement exactly what it can do, and let callers depend on exactly what they use.
useWhen: Implementations are full of empty or throwing methods
One interface serves several unrelated caller types
You want narrow, easily mocked test seams
concepts.differsFrom: ISP splits contracts by caller need; SRP splits classes by reason to change. Fixing ISP often fixes accidental LSP violations as a side effect.

steps.caption: One fat interface demands print, scan and fax from everybody.
A cheap printer must still implement fax() — so it throws at runtime.
Split the contract into small roles: Printer, Scanner, Fax.
The cheap printer now implements only Printer — nothing to fake.
A multi-function device simply implements several roles.
steps.output: callers depend only on what they use

concepts.name: D — Dependency Inversion
concepts.tagline: Depend on abstractions, not on concrete classes
concepts.analogy: A lamp plugs into a socket, not soldered to the power station. Swap the power source and the lamp never notices.
explanation: High-level policy (place an order) should not import low-level detail (MySQL, SendGrid). Both should depend on an interface owned by the high-level side.
Inverting the dependency makes the detail replaceable: an in-memory repository in tests, Postgres in production, all without touching the business rules.
useWhen: Business logic is hard to test because it hard-codes a database or HTTP client
You expect to swap a vendor (payment gateway, mail provider)
You want a clean/hexagonal architecture boundary
concepts.differsFrom: Dependency Injection is the mechanism (a framework hands you the object); Dependency Inversion is the design rule (point the dependency at an interface).

steps.caption: Without inversion the service imports the database class directly.
Define an interface that expresses what the service needs.
The service now depends on the interface only.
The database class implements it — the arrow of dependency is inverted.
Tests plug in an in-memory implementation with zero changes to business rules.
steps.output: detail is swappable, policy is stable

concepts.springNote: Constructor injection is Spring's idiomatic way to invert dependencies — the service never calls new on a detail class.

sections.title: Four pillars of Java OOP
sections.blurb: Encapsulation, Abstraction, Inheritance and Polymorphism — the four ideas every Java class is built on, explained without jargon.

concepts.name: Encapsulation
concepts.tagline: Keep the data private, expose safe operations
concepts.analogy: An ATM will not let you reach into the cash drawer. You press buttons; the machine decides what is allowed and keeps the money safe.
explanation: Fields are marked private so nobody outside the class can put them into an impossible state. Public methods become the only doors in, and each door can check the rules first.
The pay-off is that invariants live in one place: a balance can never go negative because withdraw() refuses, not because every caller remembers to check.
useWhen: A value has rules attached (non-negative balance, valid email)
You want to change the internal storage later without breaking callers
Multiple threads or modules touch the same object
concepts.differsFrom: Encapsulation hides data; Abstraction hides complexity. One is about access, the other about which concepts you expose.

steps.caption: Outside code cannot touch the balance field directly — it is private.
It must call the public method instead.
The method validates the request first.
Only a valid request is allowed to change the hidden field.

concepts.springNote: In Spring, entities encapsulate the same way: no public setters, only intention-revealing methods.

concepts.name: Abstraction
concepts.tagline: Show what it does, hide how it does it
concepts.analogy: You drive with a steering wheel and a pedal. You never think about fuel injection — the car exposes a simple idea and keeps the machinery out of sight.
explanation: An interface (or abstract class) names the capability — 'send a notification' — without saying whether it is email, SMS or a push message.
Callers depend on the idea, so a new channel can be added later without touching a single line of calling code.
useWhen: Several implementations of one capability exist or will exist
You want to test callers with a fake implementation
A third-party detail should not leak across your codebase
concepts.differsFrom: Abstraction defines the contract; Polymorphism is what happens at runtime when different classes fulfil it.

steps.caption: The service only knows the Notifier interface.
It calls notify() without knowing the channel.
Today an email implementation is wired in.
Tomorrow SMS is added — the service does not change at all.

concepts.springNote: Spring picks the implementation at startup, so swapping channels is a configuration change, not a code change.

concepts.name: Inheritance
concepts.tagline: A child class reuses and extends a parent
concepts.analogy: Every vehicle can move and has wheels. A car is a vehicle that also has doors — you describe the shared part once and add only what is different.
explanation: extends creates an is-a relationship: a SavingsAccount is an Account, so it inherits the fields and methods and may override behaviour.
Inheritance is the tightest coupling in Java. Prefer composition when the relationship is really has-a, and keep hierarchies shallow.
useWhen: Subtypes are genuinely a kind of the parent
Shared behaviour is stable and unlikely to fork
A template method needs fixed steps with variable parts
concepts.differsFrom: Inheritance reuses an implementation; an interface only shares a contract. Composition wraps another object instead of becoming it.

steps.caption: The parent holds the shared behaviour: deposit and withdraw.
SavingsAccount extends it and inherits everything for free.
It adds one new method: addInterest().
CurrentAccount extends the same parent and overrides withdraw for overdrafts.

concepts.springNote: JPA maps a Java hierarchy onto tables; SINGLE_TABLE keeps all subtypes in one table with a discriminator column.

concepts.name: Polymorphism
concepts.tagline: One call, many behaviours, decided at runtime
concepts.analogy: You tell four musicians to 'play'. Each one does something different, but you gave a single instruction.
explanation: Runtime (dynamic) polymorphism: a variable typed as the parent holds a child object, and the JVM dispatches the overridden method of the actual object.
Compile-time polymorphism is method overloading — same name, different parameter lists, chosen by the compiler.
useWhen: A loop must treat many types uniformly
You want to remove if/else chains on a type field
New variants should plug in without editing existing code
concepts.differsFrom: Overriding is resolved at runtime by the object; overloading is resolved at compile time by the argument types.

steps.caption: A list holds different shapes, all typed as Shape.
The loop makes exactly one call: shape.area().
For a Circle the JVM runs the circle implementation.
For a Rectangle the same call runs different code.

concepts.springNote: Injecting a Map of an interface type gives you every implementation, which turns a switch statement into polymorphic lookup.

sections.title: Creational patterns
sections.blurb: Five classic ways to control how objects are made: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder and Prototype.

concepts.name: Singleton
concepts.tagline: Exactly one instance, shared by everyone
concepts.analogy: A building has one reception desk. Everyone goes to the same desk instead of setting up their own.
explanation: The constructor is private, so nobody can call new. A static accessor hands out the one instance the class created itself.
The safest Java form is an enum, which the JVM guarantees to create once even across serialization and reflection.
useWhen: The object is genuinely global: a cache, a connection pool, a config registry
Creating it is expensive and the state must be shared
You can accept the testing cost of global state
concepts.differsFrom: Singleton controls how many instances exist; Factory Method controls which class is instantiated. A Spring @Bean is a singleton per container, not a global static.

steps.caption: Client A asks for the instance.
None exists yet, so it is created — once.
Client B asks later and gets the very same object back.
new Registry() is impossible — the constructor is private.

concepts.springNote: Spring beans are singletons inside the container, which gives you the sharing without the untestable static.

concepts.name: Factory Method
concepts.tagline: Let a subclass decide which object to create
concepts.analogy: A pizza chain has one recipe for taking an order, but each city branch bakes its own local style.
explanation: A base class defines the workflow and leaves one creation step abstract. Subclasses override that step to return their own product.
Callers program to the product interface, so adding a new product means adding a class, not editing a switch.
useWhen: The exact class to create depends on context or configuration
You want new variants to plug in without touching existing code
A framework needs to create user-supplied types
concepts.differsFrom: Factory Method creates one product through inheritance; Abstract Factory creates a family of related products through composition.

steps.caption: The client asks the creator to deliver, not to build.
The base class runs the shared plan and calls createTransport().
The road subclass answers with a Truck.
Swap in the sea subclass and the same plan produces a Ship.

concepts.name: Abstract Factory
concepts.tagline: Create whole families of matching objects
concepts.analogy: Order a 'Victorian' furniture set and every piece matches. Order 'Modern' and you get a different but equally consistent set.
explanation: One factory interface declares a creator method per product type. Each concrete factory produces the variant of every product that belongs together.
This makes mismatched combinations impossible: you cannot get a dark-theme button next to a light-theme checkbox.
useWhen: Products must be used together and must stay consistent
You support multiple platforms, themes or vendors
Switching the whole family should be a one-line change
concepts.differsFrom: Factory Method makes one product and usually uses inheritance; Abstract Factory makes several related products and is usually injected as an object.

steps.caption: The app asks a factory for widgets, never using new.
At startup the dark factory is chosen.
It builds a dark button and a dark checkbox together.
Switching to the light factory swaps the entire family at once.

concepts.springNote: @ConditionalOnProperty picks the whole family from one line of application.yml.

concepts.name: Builder
concepts.tagline: Assemble a complex object step by step
concepts.analogy: Ordering a sandwich: you choose the bread, then the filling, then the sauce, and only at the end do you get the finished sandwich.
explanation: Instead of a constructor with ten parameters (where nobody remembers the order), each option is a named method that returns the builder.
build() validates the combination once and produces an immutable object, so a half-configured instance never escapes.
useWhen: A constructor has many optional parameters
The object should be immutable once built
Different call sites need different subsets of fields
concepts.differsFrom: Builder configures one complex object over several calls; a Factory returns a finished object in a single call and hides which class it is.

steps.caption: Start a builder — nothing is created yet.
Each step records one choice and returns the builder again.
build() checks the combination is legal.
Only then is the finished, immutable object handed over.

concepts.springNote: Spring itself is full of builders: WebClient.Builder, RestClient.builder(), and Lombok's @Builder generates the same shape for your DTOs.

concepts.name: Prototype
concepts.tagline: Copy an existing object instead of building a new one
concepts.analogy: A photocopier: rather than rewriting the form by hand, you copy the filled template and change the two fields that differ.
explanation: The object knows how to clone itself, so callers do not need to know its class or how expensive its setup was.
Decide between a shallow copy (shares nested objects) and a deep copy (duplicates them) — sharing a mutable list is the classic bug.
useWhen: Creating from scratch is expensive (parsing, network, heavy computation)
You need many near-identical variants of a configured object
The concrete class should stay unknown to the caller
concepts.differsFrom: Prototype copies an existing instance; Builder assembles a new one from parts; Factory chooses a class to instantiate.

steps.caption: One expensive object is set up once and kept as a template.
copy() duplicates it in memory — no re-parsing, no I/O.
Each copy changes only the fields that differ.
Nested collections are copied too, so edits never leak back.

concepts.springNote: Spring's prototype scope is the same idea at container level: each request for the bean yields a new instance instead of a shared one.

sections.title: Structural patterns
sections.blurb: Seven ways to compose objects into bigger structures: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight and Proxy.

concepts.name: Adapter
concepts.tagline: Make an incompatible interface fit
concepts.analogy: A travel plug. The wall socket and your charger were never designed for each other; the adapter translates between them.
explanation: You have a class the caller needs but its method names and types are wrong. The adapter implements the expected interface and forwards each call to the existing class, converting data on the way.
Nothing inside the legacy class changes, which matters when you do not own its source.
useWhen: Integrating a third-party or legacy API
Two modules model the same idea with different types
You want the ugly translation in one file instead of everywhere
concepts.differsFrom: Adapter changes an interface you cannot change; Decorator keeps the interface and adds behaviour; Facade invents a simpler interface over many classes.

steps.caption: The client can only speak one interface: pay(Money).
The vendor SDK expects cents and a currency code instead.
The adapter implements the expected interface and converts the arguments.
It forwards the translated call to the SDK — nobody else learns the SDK's shape.

concepts.name: Bridge
concepts.tagline: Split abstraction from implementation so both can vary
concepts.analogy: A TV remote and a TV. Any remote can drive any TV because they agree on a small set of signals — you are not forced to buy a Sony remote for a Sony TV.
explanation: Without Bridge, two independent dimensions (shape × renderer, notification × channel) multiply into a class explosion: 4 × 3 = 12 classes.
Bridge keeps the two hierarchies separate and links them with composition, turning 12 classes back into 4 + 3.
useWhen: Two dimensions of variation keep multiplying subclasses
The implementation should be swappable at runtime
Platform-specific code must stay isolated
concepts.differsFrom: Adapter fixes a mismatch after the fact; Bridge is designed up front. Strategy swaps one algorithm; Bridge swaps a whole implementation hierarchy.

steps.caption: Two dimensions: kinds of notification × ways to send them.
Subclassing both would need one class per combination.
Instead the abstraction holds a reference to a channel.
Any notification now works with any channel — add either side independently.

concepts.springNote: The bridge is just constructor injection — Spring wires the implementation side without the abstraction knowing which one it got.

concepts.name: Composite
concepts.tagline: Treat a group of objects like a single object
concepts.analogy: A folder on your computer. It contains files and other folders, yet 'size' works the same on all of them.
explanation: Leaf and container both implement the same interface. A container's method loops over its children and combines their answers.
Client code becomes recursion-free: it calls one method on the root and the tree walks itself.
useWhen: Data forms a part-whole tree: menus, org charts, file systems, UI layouts
Clients should not care whether they hold one item or many
Totals or renders must aggregate down a hierarchy
concepts.differsFrom: Composite is about tree structure; Decorator wraps exactly one object to add behaviour. A decorator has one child, a composite has many.

steps.caption: size() is called once, on the root folder.
The folder asks each child for its size.
A file answers directly; a folder recurses further.
Sizes bubble back up and are summed — same method at every level.

concepts.name: Decorator
concepts.tagline: Wrap an object to add behaviour at runtime
concepts.analogy: Putting on layers of clothing. Each layer adds warmth, you can add or remove them in any order, and you are still you.
explanation: A decorator implements the same interface as the thing it wraps and holds a reference to it. It adds work before or after delegating.
Because the interface is unchanged, decorators stack: caching around logging around the real service.
useWhen: Behaviour must be added per object, not per class
Subclass combinations would explode
Cross-cutting concerns: caching, logging, retry, compression
concepts.differsFrom: Decorator adds behaviour with the same interface; Proxy controls access to the object; Adapter changes the interface.

steps.caption: The caller holds a Repository — it cannot tell how many layers there are.
The caching layer checks its map first; on a miss it delegates inward.
The logging layer records the call and delegates again.
The real repository hits the database, and the answer travels back out through each layer.

concepts.springNote: Spring AOP proxies are decorators generated for you: @Cacheable, @Transactional and @Retryable each add a layer around your bean.

concepts.name: Facade
concepts.tagline: One simple door in front of a complicated system
concepts.analogy: A hotel concierge. Taxis, tickets and restaurants involve many phone calls, but you make one request and they handle the rest.
explanation: The facade exposes a small, task-shaped method and orchestrates the many subsystem calls behind it in the right order.
Subsystem classes stay public for power users; the facade just makes the common path easy and keeps callers from learning the whole map.
useWhen: A common task needs five calls in a precise sequence
You want a boundary between layers or modules
Onboarding cost of a subsystem is too high
concepts.differsFrom: Facade simplifies many classes into one new interface; Adapter converts one existing interface; Mediator coordinates peers that talk back to it.

steps.caption: The caller makes a single request: checkout(cart).
Behind the door, stock is reserved first.
Then the card is charged.
Shipping and email follow, in order — the caller never saw any of it.

concepts.name: Flyweight
concepts.tagline: Share the identical parts instead of duplicating them
concepts.analogy: A print shop keeps one set of metal letters and reuses them across every page rather than casting new letters for each word.
explanation: State is split in two: intrinsic state is identical across many objects and gets shared; extrinsic state (position, count) is passed in per call.
A factory hands out cached instances, so a million tree sprites can reference a handful of textures.
useWhen: You hold huge numbers of similar objects and memory hurts
Most of each object's data is identical and immutable
Object creation cost dominates a hot loop
concepts.differsFrom: Flyweight shares immutable instances for memory; Singleton limits a class to one instance for coordination. Flyweights are usually many, just deduplicated.

steps.caption: A million trees are drawn — but only three kinds exist.
Each tree asks the factory for its type.
The factory returns an already-created shared object.
Only the coordinates are stored per tree, so memory collapses.

concepts.name: Proxy
concepts.tagline: A stand-in that controls access to the real object
concepts.analogy: A receptionist. You reach the executive only after they check your appointment — same person you asked for, different amount of gatekeeping.
explanation: The proxy implements the same interface as the real subject and holds a reference to it, deciding when and whether to forward the call.
Common flavours: virtual (create the expensive object lazily), protection (check permissions), remote (call across the network), caching.
useWhen: The real object is expensive to create or lives remotely
Access must be checked, throttled or logged
You need lazy loading of a heavy resource
concepts.differsFrom: Proxy controls access and usually creates or owns the subject; Decorator always has a subject and adds behaviour to it. Intent differs more than structure.

steps.caption: The client asks for the document.
The proxy checks the caller's rights first.
Denied requests never reach the real object at all.
On success the heavy object is loaded lazily — once — and the call is forwarded.

concepts.springNote: @Transactional, @PreAuthorize and JPA lazy loading are all proxies: the bean you inject is a generated stand-in around the real object.

sections.title: Behavioral patterns
sections.blurb: Eleven ways objects coordinate and share responsibility: Observer, Strategy, Command, State, Template Method, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Visitor, Chain of Responsibility and Interpreter.

concepts.name: Observer
concepts.tagline: One thing changes, many things get told
concepts.analogy: A newsletter. The publisher does not know who subscribed; anyone who signed up simply receives the next issue.
explanation: The subject keeps a list of listeners. When its state changes it walks the list and calls the same notify method on each one.
Listeners can be added or removed at runtime, and the subject never imports their classes — it only knows the listener interface.
useWhen: One event must fan out to several unrelated reactions
You want to add reactions without editing the code that emits the event
UI widgets, audit logs and emails all react to the same domain change
concepts.differsFrom: Observer broadcasts to many listeners with no reply. Mediator centralises many-to-many talk through one hub. Chain of Responsibility passes one request along until someone handles it.

steps.caption: Two listeners subscribe. The publisher only stores them in a list.
An order is placed — the publisher's state changes.
It walks the list and fires the same event at everyone.
Each listener reacts on its own. Adding a third one changes no existing code.

concepts.springNote: Spring gives you the listener list for free through ApplicationEventPublisher.

concepts.name: Strategy
concepts.tagline: Swap the algorithm, keep the caller
concepts.analogy: Choosing a route in a maps app: walking, driving or transit. The destination is the same; only the method of getting there swaps.
explanation: Each interchangeable algorithm gets its own class behind a shared interface. The caller holds the interface and never branches on a type.
Adding a new algorithm means adding a class, not editing an if-else ladder — the practical way to obey Open/Closed.
useWhen: You have a growing if/switch that picks between algorithms
The choice is made at runtime from config or user input
Each variant deserves its own tests
concepts.differsFrom: Strategy swaps how one step is done and the caller picks it. State swaps behaviour based on internal state and transitions itself. Template Method fixes the skeleton and lets subclasses fill holes.

steps.caption: Checkout needs a shipping price but must not know the formulas.
It depends only on the interface, so every formula looks identical to it.
At runtime the express strategy is injected.
Swapping to Standard later touches one line — no branching anywhere.

concepts.springNote: Injecting a Map<String, Interface> gives you every implementation keyed by bean name.

concepts.name: Command
concepts.tagline: Turn a request into an object you can queue and undo
concepts.analogy: A restaurant order slip. The waiter writes the request down; the slip can be queued, re-read, or torn up before it is cooked.
explanation: Each action becomes an object with an execute (and often undo) method, capturing the receiver and the arguments.
Because a request is now data, you can queue it, log it, retry it, schedule it or reverse it.
useWhen: You need undo/redo
Requests must be queued, retried or audited
You want to record user actions
concepts.differsFrom: Command wraps one request as an object; Strategy wraps an algorithm chosen by the caller; Memento stores state so a Command can be undone.

steps.caption: The user clicks Bold. The UI does not touch the document directly.
It creates a command object holding the action and its target.
The command runs and is pushed onto the history stack.
Ctrl+Z pops the stack and calls undo — reversal is free.

concepts.name: State
concepts.tagline: Behaviour changes when the object's state changes
concepts.analogy: A traffic light. The same pole behaves differently depending on which lamp is lit, and each lamp knows which one comes next.
explanation: Each state becomes a class implementing the same interface. The context delegates to its current state object instead of checking flags.
Transitions live inside the states, so illegal moves (ship before pay) simply have no implementation.
useWhen: An object has a lifecycle with rules about what is allowed when
You keep writing if (status == ...) in many methods
Order, ticket or subscription workflows
concepts.differsFrom: State transitions itself and the object's behaviour changes over its lifetime; Strategy is chosen from outside and does not switch itself.

steps.caption: The order starts in the New state and delegates every call to it.
ship() is called too early — the New state simply refuses.
pay() succeeds and the state object is replaced with Paid.
Now ship() is legal. The rules live in the states, not in if-ladders.

concepts.springNote: An enum with per-constant bodies is the compact JPA-friendly version of State.

concepts.name: Template Method
concepts.tagline: Fix the steps, let subclasses fill the gaps
concepts.analogy: A recipe card that says: prepare, cook, plate. Every dish follows those three beats; only the contents of each beat differ.
explanation: A final method in the base class defines the order of steps and calls abstract hooks for the parts that vary.
The skeleton cannot be reordered by subclasses, which is exactly the point when the sequence carries the correctness.
useWhen: Several flows share the same sequence but differ in a couple of steps
Import/export jobs, report generation, test fixtures
You want to guarantee the order of operations
concepts.differsFrom: Template Method varies steps through inheritance at compile time; Strategy varies the whole algorithm through composition at runtime.

steps.caption: The base class owns run() and the order of the three steps.
fetch() is a hole — the sales subclass reads the orders table.
format() is another hole — this subclass builds a CSV.
send() is shared, so no subclass can forget or reorder it.

concepts.name: Iterator
concepts.tagline: Walk a collection without exposing its insides
concepts.analogy: A TV remote's channel-up button. You move through the channels one at a time without knowing how the list is stored.
explanation: The collection returns a small cursor object with hasNext/next. Callers loop without learning whether the data is an array, a tree or a paged API.
Because the cursor is separate, several traversals can run at once and the storage can change without breaking callers.
useWhen: You expose a custom collection
Traversal should hide paging or lazy loading
Multiple independent cursors over the same data
concepts.differsFrom: Iterator is about sequential access to elements; Composite is about tree structure; Visitor adds new operations over an existing structure.

steps.caption: The client just writes a for-each loop.
The collection hands back a cursor instead of its internal list.
When page one runs out the cursor quietly fetches page two.
The loop never changes even though the storage did.

concepts.name: Mediator
concepts.tagline: Components talk through a hub, never to each other
concepts.analogy: An air traffic controller. Pilots never radio each other; everyone talks to the tower, so the rules live in one place.
explanation: Instead of n components holding references to each other, each holds one reference to the mediator, which decides who reacts to what.
Coordination logic becomes readable in a single class, and components become reusable in isolation.
useWhen: Widgets or services are wired into a tangle of mutual references
Coordination rules keep changing
Chat rooms, form widgets, workflow orchestration
concepts.differsFrom: Mediator centralises two-way coordination between known participants; Observer is a one-way broadcast where the publisher does not care who listens; Facade only simplifies access downwards.

steps.caption: The date changes. The picker tells only the mediator.
The mediator holds the rules: a new date means reload the rooms.
It refreshes the room list, then recalculates the price.
No component imports another, so each can be reused or tested alone.

concepts.name: Memento
concepts.tagline: Save a snapshot you can roll back to
concepts.analogy: A save point in a game. You keep a copy of the moment, and if things go wrong you load it back exactly as it was.
explanation: The originator produces an opaque snapshot of its own state. A caretaker stores snapshots but cannot read or edit their fields.
This preserves encapsulation: only the originator knows how to restore itself.
useWhen: Undo of complex state
Draft/checkpoint features
Transactional rollback in memory
concepts.differsFrom: Memento stores state; Command stores an action. Undo usually pairs them: a Command captures a Memento before running.

steps.caption: Before a risky edit the editor produces a snapshot of itself.
History stores it but cannot read the fields inside.
The edit goes wrong.
History hands the snapshot back and only the editor knows how to apply it.

concepts.name: Visitor
concepts.tagline: Add new operations without touching the classes
concepts.analogy: A building inspector. The rooms stay exactly as they are; different inspectors (fire, electrical, tax) walk through and each does their own job.
explanation: Elements expose an accept(visitor) method. Each visitor implements one operation per element type, so a new operation is a new class, not an edit to every element.
The trade-off is reversed: adding an operation is cheap, adding an element type means editing every visitor.
useWhen: A stable set of node types with many operations over them
Compilers, ASTs, document trees, report exporters
You do not want business logic inside the data classes
concepts.differsFrom: Visitor adds operations to a fixed structure; Composite defines that structure; Iterator only walks it. Use Visitor when types are stable and operations grow.

steps.caption: The node classes hold data and one accept() method — nothing else.
A total visitor walks the tree and adds up amounts.
A PDF visitor walks the same tree and renders it instead.
A third operation is a new class — the node classes never change.

concepts.springNote: Modern Java sealed types + switch patterns give Visitor's benefits with far less ceremony.

concepts.name: Chain of Responsibility
concepts.tagline: Pass the request along until someone handles it
concepts.analogy: A support desk. Tier 1 tries first; if they cannot solve it, the ticket moves to tier 2, then tier 3.
explanation: Handlers are linked in a line. Each either handles the request or forwards it, and no handler knows the full list.
You can reorder, insert or drop a handler without touching the sender or the other handlers.
useWhen: Validation, authentication and logging layers around a request
Escalation or approval rules
Web filters and interceptors
concepts.differsFrom: Chain gives each handler a chance to stop the request; Decorator always wraps and always delegates; Observer notifies everyone at once with no ordering.

steps.caption: An expense claim enters the chain at the first handler.
The team lead's limit is too low, so it moves on untouched.
The manager's limit is also too low — pass again.
The director can approve, so the chain stops there.

concepts.springNote: Spring Security's filter chain is Chain of Responsibility running in production.

concepts.name: Interpreter
concepts.tagline: Give a little language its own grammar of objects
concepts.analogy: A calculator that reads '2 + 3 × 4'. Each symbol becomes a small part of a tree, and evaluating the tree gives the answer.
explanation: Every grammar rule becomes a class with an interpret method. Sentences are parsed into a tree of these objects and evaluated recursively.
It suits small, stable DSLs — search filters, pricing rules, feature flags. For real languages, reach for a parser generator.
useWhen: Users need to express rules without a redeploy
You have a small grammar that changes rarely
Search filters, permission expressions, formula fields
concepts.differsFrom: Interpreter defines and evaluates a grammar; Composite is the tree shape it borrows; Visitor is often used to add operations over the same tree.

steps.caption: A user types a rule as plain text.
The parser turns each part into a small expression object.
An AND node evaluates its left and right children.
The tree returns a value — new rules need no code change.

concepts.springNote: Spring Expression Language (SpEL) is a ready-made Interpreter you can embed.

patternTable.name: Singleton
patternTable.solves: Exactly one shared instance for the whole app
patternTable.confusedWith: Static utility class — Singleton keeps state and can implement interfaces

patternTable.name: Factory Method
patternTable.solves: Let a subclass decide which single object to create
patternTable.confusedWith: Abstract Factory — that one creates whole families of objects

patternTable.name: Abstract Factory
patternTable.solves: Create matching families of related objects
patternTable.confusedWith: Factory Method — one product vs a matched set

patternTable.name: Builder
patternTable.solves: Assemble a complex object step by step
patternTable.confusedWith: Factory — Builder is for many optional parts, not type choice

patternTable.name: Prototype
patternTable.solves: Copy an existing configured object instead of rebuilding it
patternTable.confusedWith: Builder — Prototype clones, Builder constructs

patternTable.name: Adapter
patternTable.solves: Make an incompatible interface usable
patternTable.confusedWith: Facade — Adapter converts one API, Facade simplifies many

patternTable.name: Bridge
patternTable.solves: Vary abstraction and implementation independently
patternTable.confusedWith: Adapter — Bridge is designed up front, Adapter fixes after the fact

patternTable.name: Composite
patternTable.solves: Treat a tree of objects like a single object
patternTable.confusedWith: Decorator — Composite groups children, Decorator wraps one

patternTable.name: Decorator
patternTable.solves: Add behaviour to one object at runtime
patternTable.confusedWith: Proxy — Decorator adds features, Proxy controls access

patternTable.name: Facade
patternTable.solves: One simple entry point over a messy subsystem
patternTable.confusedWith: Adapter — Facade simplifies, Adapter translates

patternTable.name: Flyweight
patternTable.solves: Share immutable state across thousands of objects
patternTable.confusedWith: Singleton — Flyweight has many shared instances, not one

patternTable.name: Proxy
patternTable.solves: Stand in for an object to add lazy loading, caching or security
patternTable.confusedWith: Decorator — same shape, different intent

patternTable.name: Observer
patternTable.solves: Notify many listeners when something changes
patternTable.confusedWith: Mediator — Observer broadcasts, Mediator coordinates

patternTable.name: Strategy
patternTable.solves: Swap an algorithm at runtime
patternTable.confusedWith: State — Strategy is chosen by the caller, State changes itself

patternTable.name: Command
patternTable.solves: Turn a request into an object you can queue or undo
patternTable.confusedWith: Strategy — Command stores a request, Strategy stores a how

patternTable.name: State
patternTable.solves: Change behaviour as the object's state changes
patternTable.confusedWith: Strategy — State transitions internally

patternTable.name: Template Method
patternTable.solves: Fix the skeleton of an algorithm, let subclasses fill steps
patternTable.confusedWith: Strategy — Template uses inheritance, Strategy composition

patternTable.name: Iterator
patternTable.solves: Walk a collection without exposing its internals
patternTable.confusedWith: Visitor — Iterator moves, Visitor acts on each element

patternTable.name: Mediator
patternTable.solves: Route all communication through one hub
patternTable.confusedWith: Observer — Mediator knows everyone, Observer just publishes

patternTable.name: Memento
patternTable.solves: Snapshot and restore state without breaking encapsulation
patternTable.confusedWith: Command undo — Memento saves state, Command replays actions

patternTable.name: Visitor
patternTable.solves: Add new operations to a fixed object structure
patternTable.confusedWith: Strategy — Visitor varies by element type

patternTable.name: Chain of Responsibility
patternTable.solves: Pass a request along handlers until one deals with it
patternTable.confusedWith: Decorator — chain may stop early, decorators all run

patternTable.name: Interpreter
patternTable.solves: Evaluate sentences of a small language
patternTable.confusedWith: Composite — Interpreter is a Composite tree that evaluates
